candidates.title: 8 Home Office Accessories That Make Your Workspace Feel Less Like Work
candidates.full_text:
A home office can end up looking like a room your employer forgot to furnish. There’s the monitor, the keyboard, the cup of pens, and very little that explains who actually sits there. Making it more personal doesn’t require replacing the desk or buying another productivity system. Sometimes it’s a lamp with an improbable shape, a living object beside the screen, or something you can pick up and play with.

These eight home office accessories make room for that less dutiful side of working from home. Some help with ordinary tasks, while others simply give you something enjoyable to look at between them. The selection moves from digital characters and miniature architecture to paper, plants, and a surprisingly considered trash bin. Choose the one that suits your habits, rather than treating the whole collection as another mandatory desktop shopping checklist.

Sony’s ELF-MN1 is an announced six-inch Spatial Reality Display intended to put compatible digital figures and other detailed 3D content beside your keyboard. It uses eye tracking and tiny lenses over an LCD to direct different views toward each eye, creating depth without glasses or a headset. Sony schedules its Japanese release for December 11, 2026. The appeal is wonderfully specific: a favorite character gets a place in your workspace without becoming another physical figurine to dust or rearrange regularly.

The important distinction is that this is a display, not a hologram floating freely above the desk. It needs a compatible smartphone or PC and suitable content, so the experience depends on more than the object itself. Sony specifies viewing for one person, which suits a personal workspace better than a shared spectacle. For an anime enthusiast or digital collector, that private little stage is the point. It brings a hobby into the room without pretending to organize your afternoon.

A glowing globe appears to pause at the edge of a tiny staircase. Designed by Notchi Architects for Oblure, the Stair Table Lamp turns basic architectural geometry into something closer to a desktop prop from a playful animated film. The stepped block gives the light a visual story even before you switch it on. Beyond that expressive shape, it also incorporates two USB-C charging ports and a power outlet, putting useful connections inside its sculptural base beside your everyday equipment.

For a home office, the attraction is having a lamp you might choose for the living room rather than accept from an equipment catalog. Its stepped form can serve as a bookend, giving it a second reason to sit beside your reading material. Check electrical compatibility before ordering:

Tevaplanter puts the interesting part of growing a plant on the outside. Its porous ceramic body holds water inside, allowing moisture to pass through to roots attached to the textured exterior. There’s no potting soil concealing the process, so the vessel becomes a support for a changing patchwork of growth. Beside a monitor, that makes a useful visual contrast: one object updates in pixels, while the other changes through roots, leaves, and the occasionally unpredictable business of keeping something alive.

This belongs in a home office with room for a small growing project, rather than someone seeking greenery to ignore. The maker recommends suitable plants such as orchids and ferns, but individual species still need appropriate care. You’ll need to refill the reservoir and choose a position that meets your plant’s lighting needs. Think of it as a living desktop display with responsibilities attached. Watching that surface change is the pleasure; removing soil does not remove the work of gardening.

The TriAngular Calendar 2027 makes checking a date a small physical action instead of another reason to unlock your phone. Three months wrap around its triangular paper structure, so you rotate the calendar to see another month. There’s no separate stand underneath: the folded paper supports itself, secured with a paper clip rather than metal hardware. Silver specialty paper and white printing give this ordinary desk necessity a more deliberate presence, without adding electronics or asking you to charge anything.

Made in Japan, each sheet is silkscreen printed by hand, with white ink applied twice to the silver paper. Individual months are perforated for removal, and January and February 2028 are included beyond the main year. At 60 millimeters wide and 53 millimeters deep, its footprint is modest enough

candidates.title: SpaceX caught a Starship coming home from orbit
candidates.full_text:
Ship 42 left Starbase on Friday afternoon and spent 22 and a half hours circling Earth. On Saturday it flew home, down through the clouds and into the arms of the launch tower that sent it up.

Flight 15 was SpaceX’s first attempt to catch both halves of the rocket on a single flight, the Super Heavy booster minutes after liftoff and the ship itself a day later. The booster half failed inside six minutes. The ship half is the one that changes what a returning spacecraft can do.

The system is built around a single idea: catch both halves at the launch tower, turn them around, and fly them again without refurbishment. Flight 15 was the first attempt at the full sequence on one flight, with the ship itself as the prize.

The stack lifted off from Pad 2 at Starbase at 4:47 p.m. Texas time on Friday, all 33 Raptor engines lit on Super Heavy Booster 22. Hot-staging went cleanly, Ship 42’s six Raptors took it on toward orbit, and the booster flipped around to fly itself home. The flight plan had it back in the tower’s arms at T+6:35, six and a half minutes after it left them.

SpaceX says the boostback burn relit 32 of the 33 engines, then ended early, stopped short by low fuel mass. While the booster coasted, its guidance, navigation and control system triggered an automated abort and steered it to its offshore contingency site.

Booster 22 lit its engines once more for a landing burn over the Gulf of Mexico, came to a hover, and shut down. Its flight termination system fired and destroyed it. SpaceX says the root cause of the short burn is still under investigation, and Musk said on Sunday that the booster’s engines had slightly underperformed, leaving it short of propellant for the trip home.

Ship 42 had no such trouble. A short second burn from a single Raptor settled it into orbit about 275 kilometers up, and over the next 42 minutes it released its full payload, 26 Starlink V3 satellites. SpaceX confirmed contact with every one of them as they began climbing toward their working orbits to join the constellation. It was just the second time a Starship had reached orbit at all.

Each of those satellites adds a terabit per second of capacity, and three of them carried cameras pointed back at the ship to scan its heatshield during the long coast. The ship circled Earth about 14 times while flight controllers ran three scheduled return checks, over Hawaii, then Chile, then Hawaii again, before committing to the trip home.

SpaceX says the 26 satellites together add as much capacity as about 10 Falcon 9 launches carrying the smaller Starlink V2 Mini. The trip home was never automatic either: the ship only started down after flight control confirmed the systems needed for reentry, the landing burn and the tower approach were healthy.

SpaceX streamed the whole flight live, liftoff to catch, and for hours of the coast the ship sent down live views from its own cameras over the same Starlink network it had just added 26 satellites to.

The deorbit burn was a 10-second firing of one sea-level Raptor, enough to drop Ship 42 out of orbit and start the fall. Entry began 22 hours and 10 minutes after liftoff, the ship riding its heatshield belly-first and bleeding speed from more than 16,000 mph. Then came a final swoosh out over the Gulf before it lined up on the pad it had left the day before.

Three Raptors lit at T+22:32:16 and the ship swung upright for its landing flip, the tower’s arms closing on it at T+22:32:34, just over two minutes after it had gone subsonic at T+22:30:13. SpaceX summed it up in three words: “Mechazilla catches Starship!”

Catching the ship is the half of full reusability SpaceX had never shown. Boosters have been caught on three earlier flights, and Starship only reached orbit for the first time in September, on Flight 14. A ship that comes home to its launch tower needs no landing legs, no recovery ships and no ocean splashdown, and it lands exactly where it needs to be inspected, refueled and flown again.

None of that turnaround has been proven yet, and the booster investigation will run alongside whatever SpaceX learns from Ship 42’s scorched tiles. Musk, inspecting the ship within hours of the catch, posted that it “looks great.”

The double catch is still out there waiting, and SpaceX hasn’t announced a Flight 16 date. When both halves come home on the same flight, the loop SpaceX has been drawing for years closes. The harder half is done, though, and it was done by a spaceship that flew itself

candidates.title: Wooden Monopoly and Scrabble You’ll Actually Want to Display
candidates.full_text:
Board games are a popular way to while away the time during parties or gatherings. You just whip out whichever game everyone wants to play and then put it away when everyone has had their fill or when the party is officially over. Most of these board games are meant to be put away when no longer in use. But what if the board itself and its accessories are well designed enough that you wouldn’t mind displaying them even when no one’s playing?

WS Game Company has released the Nordic Collection, a redesign of two familiar board games: Monopoly and Scrabble. What makes these editions stand out from the versions we’re used to is their natural wood finish, as well as magnetic connections and coordinated storage.

Normally, conventional board games are unfolded when you want to play them. With this collection, you join separate wooden panels using concealed magnets. You get a wooden playing surface when the game is in use, but when you’re finished, you can separate it into smaller sections for storage. The modular construction refers to these panels; the two games are sold separately.

Since both boards have a natural wood finish, rounded forms, and minimalist graphics, you may also want to display them and make them part of your room’s aesthetic. Well, of course, only if you have space for them, since the assembled boards would need a tabletop for a full display. If you don’t, the coordinating wood storage boxes offer another way to keep the games on a shelf without leaving all the pieces out.

Monopoly Nordic Edition uses four wooden panels and comes with six die-cast metal tokens, solid wood houses and hotels, and custom-designed Chance, Community Chest, and Title Deed cards. You also have a removable wood-and-cork banker’s tray to organize the money, along with two dice that you roll for most of the game. The tray is of course very useful since with this game you have so many loose components. This way, the banker has a dedicated place to manage the cash instead of just spreading it across the table.

The houses are probably the most playful change. They’re shaped like trees and the players can stack them vertically as they develop a propert, giving your board a growing miniature forest instead of the usual rows of houses. It’s a small change that makes the Scandinavian theme part of the pieces you handle throughout the game, rather than just a finish on the box.

Scrabble Nordic Edition has a three-panel wood board, solid wood letter tiles, and four solid wood tile racks. You have a microsuede pouch to put your tiles in and you even get a scorebook with a pencil and a sand timer with wooden end caps. The materials carry through from the board to the smaller accessories, so there’s a consistent look when everything is laid out for a game, rather than the board getting all the attention.

The board also keeps a useful familiar detail: small triangular markings at the edges of premium squares. These help you see the bonus spaces even when there are tiles covering them. That’s worth keeping in a visually simplified edition, where making everything look cleaner shouldn’t mean making the game harder to read. The redesign gives the letters and scoring spaces room to remain the focus.

Both editions are listed at $200 each on WS Game Company’s US website, so this is a purchase to consider for the materials and presentation rather than simply getting a copy of either game. You’re paying for the wooden construction, coordinated accessories, and storage as much as the playing surface. If you only want to play occasionally, the decorative storage may not justify the price.

For anyone who enjoys having a game ready for guests, the appeal is easy to understand. You can leave it assembled if there’s room, or pack it into a box you don’t mind keeping visible. You still have to clear the table for dinner, but the game doesn’t necessarily have to disappear into a closet afterward.
